newsitem.title: USA: G7 deputies expected to meet on Monday in Germany.
newsitem.headline: G7 deputies expected to meet on Monday in Germany.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Deputy finance ministers from the Group of Seven are expected to meet on Monday in Frankfurt to discuss the dollar's steep rise and the health of the world economy, international monetary sources said.
The meeting is designed to pave the way and set the agenda for the February 8 gathering in Berlin of G7 finance ministers and central bank chiefs.

The sources, who declined to be named, said that meeting is likely to dwell at length on the dollar. But they voiced doubts that it would result in anything substantial to stop the dollar rise, despite some uneasiness about the pace of the advance.

One source said the G7 is preoccupied by, but not overly concerned with, the dollar's rise. Another said that the group might eventually have to act to try to rein in the greenback, but that now did not seem the time to do it.
Germany has proposed that the G7 discuss whether the current pattern of exchange rates is consistent with underlying fundamentals, the sources said.

Also on the proposed German agenda for the Berlin meeting: the world economic outlook and G7 economic policy; financial market developments and their consistency with the real economy; and the European monetary union.
The G7 is comprised of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

Japan has exhibited the most uneasiness among the group about the dollar's relentless rise, although Japanese officials admit that their policy has at times seemed ambiguous, first seeking to cap the advance, then appearing to countenance it.
Senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara seemed to take the former tack on Thursday, when he raised the possibility of currency intervention.
A source, though, said that Sakakibara privately recognizes that a further gradual rise of the dollar against the yen would be good for the Japanese economy.

Small and medium-sized Japanese firms would particularly benefit from a weaker yen, which would boost their exports. Bigger firms on the whole would also benefit, but less so than in the past because of increased direct investment abroad.

What has some Japanese officials worried, though, is the risk of a triple whammy for the economy, with a steep drop in the yen triggering declines in the stock and bond markets in a massive vote of no confidence by investors in Tokyo.
Tokyo's ambivalence about the dollar is summed up by the recent mantra of many officials there -- they oppose wide swings in exchange rates, in either direction.

Germany too has shown the first inklings of some unease about the dollar's rise, but it does not appear nearly as uncomfortable as Japan and on the whole has welcomed the strength of the U.S. currency.
Sources said that Germany would like to avoid the perception of the mark as a weak currency and have thus taken to portraying the dollar's rise as a needed correction.
"The normalization of the mark against the dollar will reach an end soon," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said earlier this week. "The mark will remain a strong currency."

Germany recognizes that the dollar's advance will give its exports a boost at a time when its domestic economy faces difficulties and its budget policy is being tightened to meet requirements for participation in European monetary union.
For its part, the United States has publicly shown no sign of altering its currency stance. "Our policy has not changed," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Thursday.

That policy avers that a strong dollar is in the best interests of the United States because it helps hold down inflation and interest rates. Rubin also believes that currency markets over time reflect fundamentals.

Traders said that has exactly been what has been driving the dollar higher. With its economy strong and its stock market buoyant, the United States looks like the best place for investors to put their money.

But that's not good news for U.S. exporters, who have recently stepped up their complaints about the dollar. Some administration officials outside of Treasury have also voiced some unease about the currency's advance, expressing worries that it will undo gains made in trade agreements with Japan.
In one sense, Rubin faces a bit of a dilemma with his strong dollar policy. The markets believe that what he wants is an ever stronger dollar.

Sources, though, said it would be difficult for Rubin to change his tune now because that could upset U.S. stock and bond markets. Instead, he is likely to focus his attention on trying to convince Europe and particularly Japan to do more to spur their economies.

Japanese officials have shown no willingness to back away from plans to sharply tighten budget policy. But the United States is likely to argue that Japan needs faster growth to make it easier for Tokyo to carry out structural reforms.
